extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in number theory; informed general readers
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedia-level exposition of Andrew Wiles's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem, describing the strategy, key intermediate theorems (Ribet, Langlands–Tunnell), deformation/R=T methods, and technical ingredients used to prove modularity for semistable elliptic curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove modularity theorem for semistable elliptic curves
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that every semistable elliptic curve over Q is modular (the Taniyama–Shimura–Weil conjecture for semistable elliptic curves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central goal of Wiles's approach: via contradiction, modularity of semistable curves implies Fermat's Last Theorem (because a Frey curve built from a hypothetical counterexample would have to be both modular and non-modular). Wiles's papers in Annals establish this for semistable curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Ribet's theorem to link Fermat to modularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Ribet's theorem (the epsilon conjecture) shows that a Frey curve constructed from a putative solution of Fermat's equation cannot be modular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combined with a proof that all semistable elliptic curves are modular, this yields a contradiction and thus proves Fermat's Last Theorem. The article emphasises Ribet's role in reducing FLT to a modularity statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associate hypothetical FLT solutions with a Frey curve
rubrics_metrics.description: Given integers (a,b,c,n) purportedly satisfying a^n + b^n = c^n (n>2), construct the corresponding Frey elliptic curve y^2 = x(x - a^n)(x + b^n) which has special arithmetic properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frey's insight is that a counterexample to FLT would produce a semistable elliptic curve with exceptional properties; showing such curves must be modular (Ribet contradicts non-modularity) is the crux of the strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modularity lifting theorem (lifting theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove that if the geometric Galois representation ρ(E,p) of a semistable elliptic curve E is modular (for some prime p>2) and satisfies technical conditions (e.g., irreducibility), then E itself is modular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiles's lifting theorem is the major technical achievement: it converts modularity of a representation at one prime into modularity of the curve, and is proven using deformation theory and commutative-algebra arguments (R→T). It also allows using any convenient prime p>2 to establish modularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Langlands–Tunnell as base case for mod 3 representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the Langlands–Tunnell theorem which implies that mod 3 irreducible Galois representations come from modular forms (i.e., are modular).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This result provides the initial modularity input for p=3 cases; Wiles uses it as the starting point of an induction/lifting argument to higher ℓ-adic powers for ℓ=3.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3–5 switch (interplay between p=3 and p=5 representations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ a trick switching between p=3 and p=5 to handle cases where the mod 3 representation is reducible: either work with p=5 directly or find an auxiliary semistable elliptic curve F so that ρ_{F,3} is irreducible while ρ_{E,5} ≅ ρ_{F,5}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 3–5 switch resolves reducible/degenerate mod 3 cases by transferring to a situation where Langlands–Tunnell (p=3) can be applied to an auxiliary curve, thereby proving modularity of the original curve via isomorphism at p=5 and the lifting theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show R = T (identify deformation ring with Hecke algebra)
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate that the deformation ring R (parametrizing certain Galois representation deformations) is isomorphic to the appropriate Hecke algebra T (an 'R=T theorem').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiles's strategy reduces modularity lifting to proving R→T is an isomorphism. He uses commutative algebra, the numerical criterion (equality/finite cardinality of two abelian groups), and congruences between Hecke rings to establish R=T (with a separate article addressing the flat case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a class number formula (CNF) for the inductive/counting step
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a class number formula (CNF) to enable counting arguments and induction on lifts of mod ℓ^n representations to ℓ^{n+1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiles attempted to derive the CNF using horizontal Iwasawa theory, then worked to extend Kolyvagin–Flach's Euler-system methods to produce the necessary CNF. The CNF is crucial for the numerics in the R=T argument and for the induction on n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Euler systems / extend Kolyvagin–Flach techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ Euler-system methods (Kolyvagin–Flach) to strengthen Iwasawa-theoretic approaches and to build the CNF needed for the inductive part of the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiles extended Kolyvagin–Flach but initially this was the point where a gap appeared in his 1993 submission; the final fix combined insights from Iwasawa theory and Kolyvagin–Flach methods, together with Taylor's collaboration, to complete the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impose sufficient local/global technical conditions on Galois representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrict attention to representations satisfying a chosen set of conditions (ordinary, flat, etc.) so that the deformation theory produces the right count of lifts and matches lifts of modular forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An essential part of the method is to choose deformation conditions that are satisfied by both representations arising from elliptic curves and those from modular forms; otherwise too many lifts exist and the counting comparison fails. Wiles defines four deformation cases, with the flat case requiring extra work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use induction on ℓ-adic level (lifting mod ℓ^n to mod ℓ^{n+1})
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove modularity at level mod ℓ^n for all n by induction, starting from the base mod ℓ result (e.g., Langlands–Tunnell for ℓ=3) and showing lifts exist/match at each stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The approach compares the number of ways to lift a mod ℓ^n Galois representation to mod ℓ^{n+1} with the number of lifts of modular forms; control of deformations and the CNF make this counting argument work (Wiles uses it especially for ℓ=3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle reducible vs irreducible representation cases separately
rubrics_metrics.description: Split the proof depending on whether ρ(E,p) is reducible or irreducible; different primes and techniques may be more effective in each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For irreducible mod 3 representations, known results give modularity and the lifting theorem yields modular curves. If mod 3 is reducible, one often passes to p=5 or constructs auxiliary curves (3–5 trick) to reduce to an irreducible case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical criterion: finiteness and equal cardinality of two abelian groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the 'numerical criterion' that the R→T map is an isomorphism exactly when two relevant abelian groups are finite and have the same cardinality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiles reduces the R=T statement to checking this finiteness/equality condition; much of the proof's commutative-algebra and counting work is aimed at verifying the numerical criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work with Galois representations rather than curves to ease counting and matching
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate the problem of matching elliptic curves and modular forms into matching their associated Galois representations, which are more amenable to lifting and counting arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This insight underlies the entire strategy: representations can be compared via deformation rings and Hecke algebras; proving modularity of representations for one prime suffices to deduce modularity of the curve via lifting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide technical labor across specialized treatments (e.g., flat deformation case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and separate harder subcases (such as the flat deformation case) and treat them with dedicated arguments or separate papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiles published a companion article (with Taylor) addressing ring-theoretic properties needed for certain deformation cases; the proof architecture modularizes hard technical components to be resolved individually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide external verification and exposition for broader mathematical acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the proof accessible to scrutiny: seek referees, present lectures, and provide expository overviews, conference proceedings, and subsequent simplifications to validate and disseminate the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiles presented lectures, submitted manuscripts for review (which revealed the initial gap), then corrected the proof and published the two Annals papers; subsequent work by other mathematicians (BCDT) extended results to all elliptic curves and produced simplifications and expository material aimed at graduate students.
